title: USC Roski Eye K12 Clinician-Vision Scientist Training Program (USC Roski Eye K12)
text:
The USC Roski Eye K12 provides three years of mentored research training to Scholars committed to pursuing
careers as independent clinician-scientists in vision research. The program engages experienced, well-
established, and productive faculty Preceptors to mentor Scholars; provides a unique curriculum individualized
to the needs of each Scholar; and makes available the rich research environment and distinct opportunities at
USC for multidisciplinary and clinically impactful research. Scholars who complete the USC Roski Eye K12 are
prepared to develop successful and independent vision science research programs.

title: Integrative multiomics prediction of fetal origins and perturbations for chILD
text:
Integrative multiomics prediction of fetal origins and perturbations for chILD
Disruptions in fetal lung development play a crucial role in the etiology and pathogenesis of childhood interstitial
lung disease (chILD); however, the precise fetal lung cell origins and molecular mechanisms underlying
individual chILD remain poorly understood, even in cases linked to known genetic variants. We will perform a
secondary data analysis of existing spatial and single cell multiomics data of human fetal lung and chILD to
develop an integrative multiomics cell atlas of fetal lung with computation models to predict fetal cell origins and
gene regulatory network perturbations for chILD. The integrated and comprehensive atlas will serve as a
valuable resource for the scientific community to study lung development and diseases, and our approach can
be applied to cell origin and driving force prediction in other contexts leveraging the abundant multiomics datasets
in this data era.

title: Imaging and Histopathology core
text: (Imaging/Histopathology) Continuing funds are requested by 18 vision scientists (holding 20 eligible NEI R01 grants) and their personnel to support three resource and an administrative core in the Department of Ophthalmology Visual and Anatomical Sciences (former Ophthalmology and Anatomy/Cell Biology Departments). The Imaging/Histopathology (I/H Core) will be directed by Dr. Susmit Suvas, an R01-funded investigator with significant imaging expertise. Together with the PI, and two research assistants, the environment and capability to conduct vision research at Wayne State University and affiliated institutions will be enhanced through prioritization of the work of NEI R01 funded investigators, their staff and students (graduate and fellows) in numerous aspects of Imaging and Histopathology. The I/H core, (in Scott Hall) is readily accessible to vision scientists, and will provide for visual function analysis, embedding, sectioning/cryosectioning and immunostaining of tissues for confocal laser scanning, light microscopy, immunofluorescence, OCT and other cell imaging analyses (e.g., cell viability and quantification of plasma membrane potential), and train in equipment use. The I/H Core will foster collaboration among NEI R01 funded investigators primarily, and at reduced priority for unfunded colleagues. Clinical and translational studies also will continue to be fostered between NEI R01 funded investigators and clinicians in the merged department (OVAS). The I/H Core also will support, at reduced priority, new investigators, and/or others (e.g., those who are seeking new research directions) or who are collecting preliminary data to be used for NEI R01 grant submission.

title: Discovery and mechanism of lipid scramblases
text:
The transport of lipid molecules from their site of synthesis inside cells to other cellular locations is essential for
life and requires dedicated machinery, which when dysregulated results in disease. We are interested in
understanding the mechanism and biology of channel-like proteins (termed scramblases) that enable lipids to
cross membranes, thereby facilitating processes as varied as blood clotting, the clearance of dying cells,
modification of proteins by sugars, and the growth of energy-producing mitochondria.

title: Sex Differences in Mechanisms of Withdrawal and Recovery of Function in Emerging Adults with Heavy Cannabis Use
text:
Regular, ongoing cannabis use is associated with persistent decrements in neuropsychological, behavioral,
and psychiatric functioning, particularly in females and adolescents and young adults (AYAs). However, it is
unclear whether cessation of cannabis use, through withdrawal and after cannabinoids are no longer present in
the body, results in recovery of neuropsychological and behavioral functioning. Here we aim to characterize
how toxicological cannabinoid and endocannabinoid biomarkers predict sex-specific neuropsychological and
behavioral outcomes in AYAs over 6-weeks of abstinence, informing preventive efforts that promote cannabis
cessation and identifying biomarker predictors of clinical outcomes during early abstinence.

title: Advanced Training at the Interface of Engineering and Oral-Craniofacial Sciences
text:
Advances in engineering approaches offer previously unimagined opportunities to advance the NIDCR 2030
vision of precision oral health for all. To harness this opportunity, a critical mass of cross-trained dentists and
engineers engaged in oral and craniofacial research are urgently needed. We will develop this workforce.

title: Impact of turbulence on blood in mechanical circulatory support
text:
In heart or lung failure, people may need circulatory support through mechanical pumps. Flow
in these systems cam lead to key changes in proteins and cells within the blood that could
simultaneously lead to bleeding or blood clots. We are investigating this process and we are evaluating
potential ways to reduce the risk for bleeding or blood clots.

title: Systems biology analysis of RNA-binding protein aggregation during cellular aging
text:
Aberrant protein aggregation is associated with many age-related diseases, such as Alzheimer’s disease and
cancer. In this project, we focus on age-dependent aggregation of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), which play key
roles in a wide variety of cellular functions and are implicated in a growing number of diseases. We will combine
innovative imaging technologies with powerful genomic and proteomic tools to perform a systems-level analysis
of RBP aggregation and its functional consequences on cell physiology and lifespan, laying the foundation for
the development of therapeutic and preventive strategies towards age-associated diseases.

title: Integrative genomic and geospatial analysis of insurance claim, biobank and GWAS summary statistics for complex traits
text:
Complex human diseases are jointly influenced by genetic and environmental risk factors. Accurately
quantifying the genetic and environmental contribution is key to unveiling the biology and informing novel
therapeutics. The proposed study seeks to develop statistical methods to jointly analyze genetic and spatially
correlated community-level environmental risk factors for a myriad of diseases of public health significance.

title: Refining Mendelian disease analysis via detection of clinically relevant repeat variants
text:
Whole genome sequencing technologies have the potential to profile all clinically relevant genetic variants
simultaneously in a single genetic test. This project aims to augment existing pipelines to include highly
relevant disease variants found in repeat regions that account for over 8% of the genome and are implicated in
a large number of Mendelian diseases.

title: DNA-TEMPLATED NIR-II POTASSIUM REPORTERS FOR NONINVASIVE IMAGING OF IONIC ACTIVITY IN DEEP TISSUE
text:
This this four-year R01 (PAR--) grant application project will develop and characterize the performance of a novel
NIR-II imaging toolkit that combines DNA-based optical potassium reporters with an in vivo imaging system for
enabling real-time and noninvasive mapping of voltage activity in small-animal models.

title: Chemical tools for developmental biology
text:
Our research program uses chemical technologies and systems-level analyses to study ontogeny and
oncogenesis. Our current studies focus on optogenetic regulators of developmental signaling pathways and
small-molecule inhibitors of aldehyde dehydrogenases associated with stemness, cancer, and spermatogenesis.

title: Unraveling nonsense-mediated mRNA decay mechanisms in cancer
text:
The proposed research holds significant relevance to public health as the developed statistical and
computational methods will unveil the regulatory mechanisms of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) in
cancers. This exploration will deepen our comprehension of tumorigenesis and tumor progression, illuminating
the path toward designing more effective targeted, and personalized treatments for cancer patients. Therefore,
the proposed research aligns closely with the NIH's mission of seeking fundamental knowledge to enhance
health and alleviate illness burdens.

title: Auditory encoding, perception, and plasticity in the deaf adult brain following inner ear gene therapy
text:
For decades, health professionals have believed that if hearing isn’t established early in life, the brain can
never catch up. We developed an approach to initiate signaling between the cochlea and the brain in deaf
adult mice through cochlear gene therapy and found that hearing abilities reached normal levels within just a
few weeks. These findings challenge the “critical period” dogma while also inviting a deeper investigation into
how adult auditory system plasticity both succeeds and fails to overwrite the effects of prolonged deafness in
early life.

title: The antigen specificity of tumor-targeting T cells in non-small cell lung cancer
text:
For a subset of patients with lung cancer, immunotherapy has led to long-lasting remissions. However, because
the majority of patients fail to respond, increasing the efficacy of immunotherapy for non-responders remains a
critical priority of cancer research. This project seeks to identify and characterize anti-tumor T cells in lung cancer
patients, to inform the development of novel therapies that enhance the anti-tumor response for treatment non-
responders.

title: Reprogramming fibroblasts embryonic origins to overcome skin fibrosis and scarring.
text:
8. Project Narrative
Scarring is the end result of injury in adult skin and results in an enormous financial and medical burden for our
society, yet no molecular therapies exist that can prevent scarring or its sequelae. Facial wounds heal with
reduced scars compared to back and abdominal scars; however, molecular drivers governing the outcome of
skin wounds derived from different embryonic origins remains unknown. Therefore, we will explore the
biomolecular and tissue mechanical drivers of facial skin healing in order to facilitate development of novel
targets to minimize scarring and promote regenerative wound healing.

title: Spatiotemporal Control of Cerebral Blood Flow by Purinergic Signaling Networks
text:
Dementia affects over 55 million people worldwide and is projected to double in prevalence within two decades,
with vascular dysfunction implicated in at least half of all cases. This project investigates how ATP-mediated
purinergic signaling regulates neurovascular coupling and supports cognitive function. Understanding these
mechanisms will uncover new therapeutic targets for age-related cognitive decline and vascular dementia.

title: High-Content Analysis Core
text: ABSTRACT – CORE A Our Center proposes to study a large number of domain mutations and previously uncharacterized NDD- associated genetic variants in TRIO and SYNGAP1 using a high-throughput strategies (Project 1), to perform functional screens for newly developed chemical probes in mouse neurons (Project 1), and to generate novel iPSC-derived neuronal models (Project 2). All of these research endeavors will rely heavily upon efficient medium or high-throughput screening capabilities as well as the ability to analyze a multitude of phenotypes in dozens of conditions. Core A will provide the following services: 1) assist Projects 1 and 2 with the optimization of imaging strategies, MEA recordings, and analysis of cultured neuron systems; 2) perform high-content imaging (HCI) of neuroarchitectural phenotypes for Projects 1 and 2; 3) perform multielectrode array (MEA) analysis of neuronal network electrophysiological phenotypes for Projects 1 and 2; 4) provide instruction of Center users for HCI, MEA recordings, and analysis; 5) facilitate the offline analysis of data; 6) facilitate the storage of phenotypic data; 7) ensure quality control of data and analysis. To accomplish this work in an efficient, cost-effective, and rigorous manner, Core A will exploit standardized high-throughput workflows that unite innovative technologies with economies of scale. The Specific Aims of Core A are: Aim 1. To assess the impact of SNVs in TRIO and SYNGAP1 on neuroarchitecture and network activity in mouse neurons. Aim 2. To assess the impact of chemical modulators of GEF and GAP activity on neuroarchitecture and network activity in mouse neurons. Aim 3. To assess the impact of genetic mutations and chemical probes on human iPSC-derived neuronal models.

title: Acetylation modulates T cell receptor signaling
text:
Title: Acetylation modulates T cell receptor signaling
PA-25-301 NIH Research Project Grant (Parent R01 Clinical Trial Not Allowed)
This project will investigate the role of acetylation as a novel biologic process that modulates T cell receptor
signaling. We will explore this problem by analyzing mice deficient in Sirt2, the protein deacetylase that regulates
acetylation as well as genetically engineered human T lymphocytes isolated from melanoma and lung cancer
patient tumor samples or human TCR-T therapy targeting NY-ESO1+ melanoma and lung cancer. Our studies
will guide the development of novel strategies to break T cell anergy and exhaustion, and thus enhance the
capacity of these T cell therapeutics to cure immunotherapy resistant cancers.

title: Effects of Pain on Laboratory Drinking Topography and Daily Drinking in People with Chronic TMD Pain
text:
Individuals with chronic temporomandibular disorder (TMD) pain are at increased risk for alcohol-related
consequences compared to those without pain, and growing evidence suggests pain is a potent motivator for
alcohol use in many individuals. However, few systematic examinations of modifiable and non-modifiable risk
factors, including orofacial pain status, have been conducted. This project addresses this gap in knowledge by
determining the effect of pain on drinking topography in heavy drinkers with and without chronic TMD pain in
both the laboratory and daily life.
